newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria's growth structure still frail - council.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's growth structure still frail - council.

text.p: Algeria's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 4.0 percent in 1996, the third consecutive year of growth, but the growth structure remains shaky, a semi-official think tank said.

"The performance gives ground for satisfaction although the growth structure shows a relative vulnerability of the national economy," said the Social and Economic National Council in a report assessing the Algerian economy.
It said growth was mainly due to a bumper cereal harvest and higher crude oil prices in the international market.

"The GDP, without counting the oil, gas and agricultural sectors, would have grown only by 1.0 percent in 1996 and 1.5 percent in 1995," the council said a summary of its report published on Monday by the Algerian newspaper Liberte.
The Algerian government said it expects GDP to rise by a real 5.0 percent in 1997 against 4.0 percent in 1996 and 3.8 percent in 1995.
It said it had laid the conditions for sustained growth, including a tamed inflation which would average nine percent in 1997 against 18 percent in 1996 and 29.8 percent in 1995.

The council, however, raises alarm bells over the continuing stagnation of the non-oil and gas industry and over the social situation of ordinary Algerians as the country reforms its former state-run economy.

"Industrial activity is still in the recessionary stage and the objectives (set by the government) have not been achieved," said the council, adding that industrial production slumped 4.1 percent in the second half of 1996.

"The improvement in industrial production witnessed in the second half of 1995 with a 0.5 percent growth was completely annihilated by 1996's constraints and difficulties which continue to weigh on the sector," said the report without giving further details.

The report hailed Algeria's macro-economic performance in 1996 when the budget had a surplus of 60 billion dinars ($1.07 billion), the trade balance was at $4.5 billion and the foreign currency reserves stood at $4.2 billion.

But the CNES said "economic growth is still shaky because it still strongly depends on exogenous factors like rain levels, trends of crude oil prices and the dollar value compared to a basket of currencies".
The CNES said sustained reforms had badly affected ordinary people's welfare and that some contagious diseases like tuberculosis, eradicated in the 1970s, had reappeared.

The average purchasing power among the country's 29 million people shrank by 4.0 percent in 1996, while the number of unemployed people stood at 2.2 million, or 28.1 percent of the roughly six million workforce. More than half of the unemployed were young people aged between 20 and 24 years, it said.
The building sector completed 112,285 housing units in 1996, 14.6 percent fewer than in 1995, the council said. Algeria has a shortage of about one million housing units.

The Algerian government has been battling Moslem guerrillas since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a huge lead. Officials say poverty, lack of jobs and housing pushed many young people into the ranks of the fundamentalist rebels.
About 60,000 people have been killed in Algeria's five years of violence.
